lead: On this fourth Sunday of the Resurrection, kept as the World Prayer Day for Vocations, the readings move from sorrow to joy. Isaiah hears Zion say, “The Lord has forsaken me,” and God answers that a mother may forget her nursing child, “yet I will not forget you.” In Acts, the Holy Spirit is given in Samaria through the laying on of the apostles' hands, and Simon learns that God's gift cannot be bought. Ephesians tells those who were dead in sin that God, rich in mercy, has made them alive and seated them with Christ. In John, Jesus promises that the disciples' pain will turn into joy, like the joy of a mother when her child is born.

The thread is a gift no one can earn or seize: God's faithful love, the Spirit, salvation by grace, a joy no one can take away. Vocations belong to the same order: a call is received, never bought. The calendar notes the fuller passages Ephesians 1:15–2:7 and John 16:16–33; the exegesis follows the readings as listed.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC, after Jerusalem and its Temple had been destroyed. Many scholars attribute these chapters to a prophet of the exile writing in the tradition of Isaiah. They open with the words “Comfort, O comfort my people” (40:1).

In our passage the city of Zion, Jerusalem, is pictured as a woman: a wife who thinks herself abandoned and a mother who has lost her children. God answers her complaint, and the answer grows into a vision of the city crowded with returning children, carried by the nations.
str: v. 13: a call to heaven and earth to rejoice: the Lord has comforted his people.
v. 14: Zion's complaint: forsaken, forgotten.
vv. 15–16: God's answer: more faithful than a mother; Zion inscribed on his palms.
vv. 17–21: the ruins filled with children; the bereaved mother astonished.
vv. 22–23: the nations carry Zion's sons and daughters home; those who wait for the Lord shall not be put to shame.
kw: The Hebrew word for compassion is related to reḥem, womb. In v. 15 the two meet: “show no compassion for the child of her womb”. God's mercy is described with the most tender bond we know.
To cut into a surface so that it cannot be erased. God has not merely written Zion's name down; he has engraved it on his own hands.

A guardian who carries a child (compare Numbers 11:12, where Moses complains that he must carry the people “as a nurse carries a sucking child”). In v. 23 kings become foster fathers to Zion's children.
vv: For the Lord has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones.
The song of joy comes before the complaint. God's comfort is announced first, as Easter is announced to disciples still in grief.
The Lord has forsaken me, my Lord has forgotten me.
Scripture lets Zion say this aloud. Complaint, too, can be prayer, as in the Psalms.
Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
God does not deny that human love can fail. He says that his own love does not.
See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.
Christians can hardly hear this verse without thinking of the risen Lord, who showed his disciples his hands (John 20:20, 27).
Who has borne me these?
The barren mother finds herself surrounded by children she did not expect. It is a picture of the Church gathered from the nations.
those who wait for me shall not be put to shame.
The image before it, of kings bowing and licking the dust, is the court language of the ancient world for complete submission. The promise at the end is the point: waiting on God is never wasted.
ch: The Catechism quotes verses 14–15 to show that God's love for his people is stronger than a mother's love for her children (CCC 219), and it teaches that God's parental tenderness can be expressed by the image of motherhood, though God is neither man nor woman (CCC 239; 370). Pope John Paul I said in a brief Angelus of 1978 that God is our Father, and even more our Mother (in substance). The Church has also seen in the crowded city of vv. 18–23 a picture of herself, the Mother of many children, gathered from all peoples.

set: After the death of Stephen, a persecution scattered the believers from Jerusalem (8:1). Philip, one of the Seven chosen in Acts 6:5, went down to Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. Many believed and were baptised, among them Simon, a man who had amazed the city with magic (8:9–13).

Samaritans and Jews were long divided over the place of worship and the Scriptures (compare John 4:9, 20). That the word of God was received in Samaria was a great step outward, as the risen Lord had foretold: “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8).
str: vv. 14–17: the apostles send Peter and John; prayer and the laying on of hands; the Spirit is received.
vv. 18–19: Simon offers money for the power to give the Spirit.
vv. 20–23: Peter's rebuke and call to repentance.
v. 24: Simon asks for prayer.
v. 25: the apostles preach in many Samaritan villages on the way home.
kw: The laying on of hands is a gesture of blessing and of handing on in Scripture. Here it is joined to prayer for the gift of the Spirit.
A gift given without payment. Luke uses it of the Holy Spirit in Peter's Pentecost sermon (2:38). By its nature a gift cannot be bought.
The phrase recalls Deuteronomy 29:18, a root that bears “poisonous and bitter growth”: a heart turned away from God. The POC renders the sense as deep resentment.
vv: prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit
The apostles begin with prayer. The Spirit is asked for, not produced.
Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
John, who once wanted fire from heaven on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54), now brings the Holy Spirit to Samaritans.
May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain God’s gift with money!
From Simon's name comes the word simony: buying or selling spiritual things.
your heart is not right before God.
Peter goes to the root. The money is a symptom; the heart that wants to possess holy power is the illness.
Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may happen to me.
Luke leaves the story open. Simon at least asks for the apostles' prayer.
ch: The Catechism reads this passage as a witness to the sacrament later called Confirmation: from the time of the apostles, the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of Baptism was given by the laying on of hands (CCC 1288; 1315). It names Simon's sin: simony is the buying or selling of spiritual things (CCC 2121). St Irenaeus counted Simon as the father of heresies (Against Heresies 1.23), and St Cyril of Jerusalem warned those preparing for Baptism that Simon came to the water and was baptised but was not enlightened, because his heart was not open (Procatechesis 2, in substance).

set: Ephesians is one of the letters whose authorship is discussed: tradition and many scholars hold it to be Paul's, written from prison, while others think it was written by a disciple in his name. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

In chapter 1 the letter has blessed God for choosing, adopting and redeeming us, and has prayed that we may know the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20). Now it shows that the same power has worked in us: the God who raised Christ has raised us, who were dead.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead in trespasses, following the world and the evil one, children of wrath.
v. 4: the turn: “But God”.
vv. 5–6: what God has done: made alive, raised up, seated with Christ.
v. 7: why: to show the riches of his grace in the ages to come.
kw: God's wealth is mercy. Pope John Paul II took the title of his encyclical on the mercy of God, Dives in Misericordia (1980), from this verse.
Three verbs in vv. 5–6 begin with the Greek prefix for “with”: made alive with, raised with, seated with. What happened to Christ at Easter has happened to us with him.
by grace you have been saved
The verb is in the perfect tense: a past act whose effect lasts. Salvation is God's gift; the letter repeats it in v. 8.
vv: You were dead through the trespasses and sins
Not merely weak or sick, but dead. The dead cannot raise themselves.
But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us
Two words that turn the whole story. Everything after them is God's work.
made us alive together with Christ
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
The verbs are past. In Baptism our life is already joined to the risen Lord, though we still await its full revealing (Colossians 3:3–4).
the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
ch: The Council of Trent drew on verse 3, “by nature children of wrath”, in its teaching on the state of humanity after Adam's sin (Session 6, chapter 1). The Catechism teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God, the undeserved help he gives us to respond to his call (CCC 1996). Easter is the feast of this passage: the Church baptises in the season of the Resurrection because Baptism is our rising with Christ (Romans 6:4).

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: These words belong to the Last Discourse, spoken by Jesus at the supper on the night before he died (John 13–17). He has told his disciples that he is going to the Father and that the Advocate will come (16:5–15). Now he speaks of a short absence and a return.

The Church reads these words in the season of the Resurrection because they were fulfilled at Easter: the disciples did not see him while he lay in the tomb, and then they saw him again, and their grief became joy (20:20).
str: v. 16: the riddle: “a little while”.
vv. 17–19: the disciples' puzzled questions, and Jesus' awareness of them.
v. 20: weeping and joy.
v. 21: the image of a woman in labour.
v. 22: “I will see you again”: a joy no one can take.
vv. 23–24: asking the Father in Jesus' name.
kw: The phrase occurs seven times in vv. 16–19. The disciples cannot understand it; the reader knows it means the three days between death and Resurrection, and also the whole time until the Lord comes again.
Grief and pain of body and heart. The same word is used of the woman in labour (v. 21): the sorrow is real, but it is the sorrow of a birth.

Verse 23 uses two different verbs: “you will ask (erōtaō, question) nothing of me”, but “if you ask (aiteō, request) anything of the Father”. On that day the disciples will no longer need to question him; they will be able to ask the Father directly in his name.
vv: A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.
you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
Not replaced by joy, but turned into it. The same Cross that caused the grief becomes the source of the joy.
When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come.

“Hour” is the word John uses for the Lord's Passion (12:23; 13:1). The prophets compared the birth of God's new people to a woman in labour (Isaiah 26:17; 66:7–9). Many interpreters also think here of the Mother of Jesus, whom he calls “Woman” at the Cross (19:26), and of the new family born there.
but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
Earlier he said “you will see me”; now, “I will see you”. The joy rests not on our sight of him, but on his faithful gaze upon us.
Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
Prayer in his name is the place where Easter joy grows.
ch: St Augustine read the “little while” as the whole of this present age, short when seen from its end: now we grieve because we long for the Lord and do not yet see him, but soon we shall see him, and there no one will take our joy away (Tractates on John 101, in substance). The Catechism teaches that there is no other way of Christian prayer than Christ, and that our prayer has access to the Father only if we pray in the name of Jesus (CCC 2664).

qa: Why had the Samaritans not received the Holy Spirit when they were baptised?

Luke does not explain it fully. He shows that the new community in Samaria was joined to the apostles of Jerusalem, so that the Church remained one, and that the gift of the Spirit came through their prayer and the laying on of their hands. The Catechism sees here the origin of the sacrament that completes Baptism (CCC 1288; 1315). In the Eastern Churches, including the Syro-Malabar Church, this anointing is given together with Baptism, and the oil used is consecrated by the Major Archbishop, which keeps the link with the apostles (CCC 1290–1292).
Does God really compare himself to a mother?

Yes. Isaiah does so here and again in 66:13. God is neither man nor woman; he is pure spirit, and the perfections of both father and mother are found in him (CCC 239; 370). Scripture and the Church call God Father, as Jesus taught us, and the image of a mother shows the tenderness of that same love.
If we ask anything in Jesus' name, why are some prayers not answered as we hope?

To ask in his name is to ask as he would ask, in union with his will. The Catechism speaks honestly of the trial of prayer that seems not to be heard, and reminds us with James that we may ask wrongly (CCC 2735–2737). The Father always gives what is truly good, and above all the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13).
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church keeps this Sunday, like the universal Church, as the World Prayer Day for Vocations. Our families have given many priests and religious to the Church in India and far beyond. Isaiah's barren mother, astonished at her children, and Simon's attempt to buy what can only be received, together teach the right spirit: a vocation is a gift received in prayer, and for priests through the laying on of hands; it is never a career to be acquired.

In our tradition the newly baptised child is anointed with the holy oil (Mooron) at the same celebration, so that the gift of the Spirit that Peter and John brought to Samaria is given at the very start of Christian life. The Queen of Heaven is prayed until Pentecost; with it we greet Mary, the Mother whose sorrow at the Cross was turned into the joy of the Resurrection.
study: Zion said, “The Lord has forgotten me.” When have I felt forgotten by God, and what does it mean to me that my name is written on his hands?
Simon wanted to own the power of the Spirit. In what ways can I treat holy things, roles in the parish or the Church itself as something I possess?
Ephesians says that I have been raised and seated with Christ. How would my week be different if I believed this was already true of me?
What sorrow in my family could the Lord turn into joy? Whom in my family or parish will I pray for this week, that they may hear and answer God's call?
